explanations.explanation: Paul says, "On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up…" (1 Corinthians 16:2). Starting on day one means the giving comes before the week has a chance to spend it for you. A little at a time, and nobody scrambling when Paul shows up. That's a plan even I could stick to, and I once forgot a whole batch in the oven.

You've got the weekly rhythm, friend, but the text says the first day, not the last. Paul says to set aside a portion on "the first day of every week" (1 Corinthians 16:2). The last day of the week is when I'm checking the bottom of the cookie jar and finding crumbs. Starting at the front means there's something to set aside.

The weekly part is right, but the day isn't. Paul says "the first day of every week" (1 Corinthians 16:2). He has them set something aside right at the start, saving it up as the days go by. By the time you get to the seventh day, I'd already be wondering where my portion went.

Paul says, "…I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem." (1 Corinthians 16:3). So the Corinthians do the recommending, and Paul sends letters along with the ones they pick. I like that. The people who know their own folks get to say who's trustworthy.

Soldiers make for a dramatic scene, friend, but the text doesn't mention any. Paul says he will send letters "with those you recommend" to carry the gift (1 Corinthians 16:3). The carriers are people the Corinthians recommend. No armor, no swords, just letters and trusted people.

Close, because Paul is involved, but he isn't the one choosing. He says he will send letters "with those you recommend" (1 Corinthians 16:3). The Corinthians do the recommending, and Paul's letters go with them. The text doesn't say the carriers are elders.

Paul says the people the Corinthians recommend will "carry your gift to Jerusalem" (1 Corinthians 16:3). That's the destination for the gift for the saints. Pack light, friend, it's a long walk with an offering.

Antioch is a real place, but it's not where this gift is headed. Paul says the people the Corinthians recommend will "carry your gift to Jerusalem" (1 Corinthians 16:3). Good thing for the carriers that the text is clear about the address. Nobody wants a delivery sent to the wrong door.

Damascus is a real place too, but the text sends this gift somewhere else. Paul says it goes "to Jerusalem" (1 Corinthians 16:3). The carriers are the people the Corinthians recommend, and Jerusalem is where they're going. I'd have the delivery driver double-check that address.

Paul says, "And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me." (1 Corinthians 16:4). Notice the "if." Paul leaves it open, and he doesn't say he's definitely going. If it works out, they all travel together.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, "And if it is advisable for me to go also, they can travel with me." (1 Corinthians 16:4). He doesn't say he's definitely going, only that if it's advisable, they can travel together. So the text says yes to company on the road.

explanations.answer: Help him on his journey wherever he goes
explanations.explanation: Paul says he may stay awhile, or even spend the winter, "so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go." (1 Corinthians 16:6). That's the hope he states. A good visit, and then a send-off with a little help for the road.

explanations.answer: Keep the collection safe until spring
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about keeping the collection until spring. Paul says he may stay awhile or spend the winter "so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go." (1 Corinthians 16:6). What he hopes for is help on his journey. The gift's trip is a separate plan in verse 3.

explanations.answer: Give him a house to stay in for good
explanations.explanation: A house for good would be a lot to ask, and Paul doesn't ask it. He says he may spend the winter, "so that you can help me on my journey, wherever I go." (1 Corinthians 16:6). He's talking about a stay and then moving on. Even I got to stay in a bakery of my own only because somebody gave me room.
Paul says, "I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits." (1 Corinthians 16:7). He makes his plans and he holds them with open hands. I like that, friend. I plan my batches the same way.

That's a sensible guess, since the collection is on his mind. But the condition Paul names is different: "if the Lord permits" (1 Corinthians 16:7). The collection plan is its own thing back in verse 2. This hope of spending some time with them hangs on the Lord.

Winter does come up, since Paul says he might even spend it with them (1 Corinthians 16:6). But he never makes the weather his condition. He says, "I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits." (1 Corinthians 16:7). Rain or shine, that's the one he names.

Paul says a great door for effective work has opened to him in Ephesus, "even though many oppose me." (1 Corinthians 16:9). So the text says that many oppose him. The door is open and the opposition is there too. Both are in the same verse.

That's right, friend. Paul says, "…a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me." (1 Corinthians 16:9). So there is opposition, and he stays anyway. A great door and many opponents, side by side in one verse.

explanations.answer: He is doing the work of the Lord like Paul
explanations.explanation: Paul says to see to it that Timothy has nothing to fear, "for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am." (1 Corinthians 16:10). That's the reason in the text. Timothy's work is the same work Paul is doing.

explanations.answer: He is carrying the gift for the saints
explanations.explanation: The gift does come up in this chapter, but not as the reason for Timothy. Paul says to see that Timothy has nothing to fear, "for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am." (1 Corinthians 16:10). The text doesn't say Timothy carries anything. The reason is his work.

explanations.answer: He is Paul's own brother by birth
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about Timothy being Paul's brother by birth. Paul gives the reason this way: "for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am." (1 Corinthians 16:10). It's about the work they share. Family ties aren't mentioned.

Paul says, "No one, then, should treat him with contempt." (1 Corinthians 16:11). Contempt is looking down on someone, and Paul says don't do it. He follows that with sending Timothy off in peace. I've been looked down on in a junk drawer, friend, and I wouldn't wish it on a guest.

Favor sounds nice, but it's not the word in the verse. Paul says, "No one, then, should treat him with contempt." (1 Corinthians 16:11). He names what to avoid, and it's contempt. Then he says to send Timothy on his way in peace.

Patience is a good thing, but it isn't the word Paul uses. He says, "No one, then, should treat him with contempt." (1 Corinthians 16:11). It's a warning against looking down on Timothy. The text then moves on to sending him off in peace.

The text says something different, friend. Paul says, "Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers." (1 Corinthians 16:11). So Timothy is sent off, not kept. Paul is expecting him back.

That's right. Paul says, "Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers." (1 Corinthians 16:11). He's expecting Timothy back, so the Corinthians are to send him off, not keep him. A good host knows when to pack the snacks and wave goodbye.

explanations.answer: Not now but he'll go when he has the chance
explanations.explanation: Paul says Apollos "was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity." (1 Corinthians 16:12). So it's a not now, with a promise of later. Paul asked strongly and still left room for Apollos' answer. I'd say that's how a good friend handles a no for now.

explanations.answer: Yes and he'll leave with the brothers right away
explanations.explanation: Paul did strongly urge him, but Apollos wasn't ready to go yet. The text says, "He was not at all inclined to go now…" (1 Corinthians 16:12). So there's no leaving right away. Paul says he will go when he has the opportunity.

explanations.answer: No and he never plans to go back there
explanations.explanation: It's not a flat no forever. Paul says Apollos "was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity." (1 Corinthians 16:12). The word that matters is "now." He plans to go later when the chance comes.

Paul says Stephanas and his household "were the first converts in Achaia" (1 Corinthians 16:15). They were the first people there to believe. Then Paul says they "have devoted themselves to the service of the saints." First in line and still serving.

Teachers is a reasonable guess, but it's not the word in the text. Paul says they "were the first converts in Achaia" (1 Corinthians 16:15). He then adds that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. The first part is about being first to believe.

The text doesn't call them elders. Paul says Stephanas and his household "were the first converts in Achaia" (1 Corinthians 16:15). Converts are the first people there to believe. Their serving comes right after in the same verse.

explanations.answer: Submit to them and every fellow worker
explanations.explanation: Paul urges the brothers "to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer." (1 Corinthians 16:16). So the call goes beyond Stephanas's household to every fellow worker and laborer. The people who serve are the ones worth following. I'd follow anybody who has been up since dawn doing the dishes.

explanations.answer: Pay them wages from the collection
explanations.explanation: The text says nothing about wages. The collection in this chapter is for the saints (1 Corinthians 16:1). What Paul urges about these servants is "to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer." (1 Corinthians 16:16). That's the treatment he asks for.

explanations.answer: Send them out to start new churches
explanations.explanation: Starting new churches sounds exciting, but the text doesn't say it. Paul urges the brothers "to submit to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer." (1 Corinthians 16:16). It's about how to treat people who serve. And he extends it to every fellow worker and laborer.

Paul says, "For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well." (1 Corinthians 16:18). So these three men did good for Paul and for the Corinthians too. Some people walk in and the whole room gets lighter. A fresh batch of cookies does the same thing for me.

Tested doesn't fit what the verse says. Paul says, "For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well." (1 Corinthians 16:18). Refreshed is the word, and it's a good one. These men lifted spirits instead of testing them.

Troubled is the opposite of what Paul says. He writes, "For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well." (1 Corinthians 16:18). These three men brought something good to Paul and to the Corinthians. Then he tells the Corinthians to show their appreciation.

Paul says, "Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men." (1 Corinthians 16:18). They refreshed his spirit and the Corinthians', so appreciation is the answer he gives. A thank-you goes a long way, friend. Nobody ever told me no to a thank-you.

This one is actually true. Paul says, "Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men." (1 Corinthians 16:18). He says it right after telling them these men refreshed his spirit and theirs. So he does tell them to show appreciation.

Paul says, "Greet one another with a holy kiss." (1 Corinthians 16:20). It's right after the brothers with him send their greetings. That's how he tells them to greet each other. A warm hello, and it's in the text.

This one is true, friend. Paul says, "Greet one another with a holy kiss." (1 Corinthians 16:20). It's part of the final greetings, right after all the brothers with him send theirs. So it's in the text.

explanations.answer: The grace of the Lord Jesus and Paul's own love
explanations.explanation: Paul closes with, "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you." Then he adds, "My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen." (1 Corinthians 16:23-24). Grace first, then his own love for all of them. That's a warm way to end a letter, even after a hard line.

explanations.answer: Safe travels for the gift to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: The gift's trip does come up earlier in the chapter (1 Corinthians 16:3). But Paul doesn't close with a wish for safe travels. He says, "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen." (1 Corinthians 16:23-24).

explanations.answer: Patience as they wait for Timothy
explanations.explanation: Timothy is mentioned earlier, in verses 10 and 11. But the sign-off isn't about waiting for him. Paul says, "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen." (1 Corinthians 16:23-24). Grace and love are what he leaves them with.
